Most marketers still can't tell their own writing from AI.

That's not an insult. 
It's what happens when you use a tool without knowing what it's actually doing to your output.

The AI writing problem isn't that it sounds bad.

It's that it sounds the same.

Every piece follows the same rhythm. 
Same structure. 
Same words. 
"Pivotal." 
"Groundbreaking." 
"Serves as".
The sentences are clean. 
The logic holds. 
But there's no texture. 
No friction. 
No evidence that a real person sat down and thought about this.

And readers feel it before they can name it.

I spent the first part of my career at a global beauty brand running campaigns at scale. 
We had writers. 
Good ones. 
When AI arrived, the first drafts coming back were faster, but something felt off. 
The content passed spell-check and logic-check.
But it failed the gut check every time.

It took me longer than I'd like to admit to figure out why.

AI doesn't write badly. 
It writes predictably.

There are 29 patterns it falls back on. 
This infographic maps all of them.

The ones that keep showing up in my own drafts:

→ Significance inflation: 
"Pivotal moment." 
"Testament to"
Just say what happened.

→ Vague attributions: 
"Experts say." 
"Research shows." 
Name the source or cut the claim.

→ Em dash overuse: 
One comma. 
One full stop. 
Done.

→ Sycophantic openers: 
"Great question!" 
Just answer it.

→ Filler phrases: 
"Worth noting." 
"Important to remember." 
Start after the filler.

→ Excessive hedging: 
"Could potentially." 
"Might possibly." 
Make a call.

→ AI sign-offs: 
"Hope this helps." 
"Let me know." 
End with a next step or nothing.

→ Generic conclusions: 
"The future looks bright." 
State your actual conclusion in one sentence.

→ Rule of three: 
"Innovation, inspiration, and integrity." 
Pick two. 
Or one.

→ Copula avoidance: 
"Serves as".
"Functions as". 
Just use "is".

The fix for most of these is the same: say less and say it directly.

After 16 years in marketing, 
The discipline I've found most valuable has nothing to do with tools. 
It's the willingness to cut the line that sounds good but means nothing.

AI gives you a first draft.

Dorr got to see his idea achieve scale before he passed away in 1962.

Today, we all drive next to that line and take it for granted. Self-driving trucks are about to start using it as one of their navigational inputs. Dorr couldn't have known, but he believed in the value of his invention and never gave up.
